pages.title: WELCOME TO GERMAN ROOTS
content: Sunshine. Breakfast. Homework. House, drink,
eat, fight, begin, understand. Short words,
blunt words, the words you think in. They
were here before 1066, before the Normans,
before the Latin layer settled on top: the
English of the Anglo-Saxons, still the bones
of the language.
Most of them are built from plain parts.
Break + fast. Sun + shine. Fore + cast. Learn
a part once and every word that carries it
opens before you look it up.
This pack teaches that oldest layer, a
thousand words, and on every card the
French word that came to stand beside it.
You need no German. You need to notice.

pages.title: HOW A CARD WORKS
content: The front shows a word. Press a key and the
card opens in stages: a sentence that uses
it, its DEFINITION, a second example built
on a related word, and, on 8, the notes.
The notes show the parts and what each part
means, then the word's neighbours: the
NORMAN twin, the French word that took the
court and the courtroom (begin beside
commence, cow beside beef), and, where it
helps, the German cousin the word still has
across the water. That cousin is shown, never
spoken: this is an English pack.
Rate the card 0 to 5 when it is open. The
boss fight asks the definition and offers
eight words; the synonyms and antonyms in
the notes are the clues you take with you.
TIER 1 is the plain compounds and the first
prefixes: be-, fore-, out-, over-, under-,
mis-. TIER 2 is the opaque compounds, whose
seams have healed over, and un- and up-.
TIER 3 is the doublets: the plain word and
its French twin side by side, and the
register each one carries. TIER 4 is the
phrasal verbs, the living layer of speech.
TIER 5 is the reader's English: loanwords,
calques, survivals, suffixes, kennings,
Grimm's Law and false friends.
Every cluster opens with a short lesson
naming its parts.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: breakfast, sunshine,
homework.
BE- is Old English bi, by. Set on a verb it
turns the action onto a thing: to moan is to
complain, to bemoan is to complain of. Set on
a noun or an adjective it makes a verb: to
befriend, to belittle, to benumb.
bemoan      be + moan
befriend    be + friend
bewilder    be + wilder, to lose one's way
besmirch    be + smirch, a stain
Half the verbs here have a French twin that
took the formal work: bemoan beside lament,
behold beside observe, bereave beside
deprive. The be- word is older and blunter.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: be- words.
A plain compound is two words set side by
side with no glue between them. The second
word is the thing, the first tells which
kind: a handbook is a book, the kind that
fits in the hand. Read the last part first.
handbook    hand + book
household   house + hold, those held in it
clockwork   clock + work
staircase   stair + case, an enclosure
The French twins here are the office words:
homework beside assignment, hallway beside
corridor, gateway beside portal. The plain
word names the thing you can touch.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: house and workshop words.
FORE- is Old English fore, before, in front.
On a verb it sets the action ahead of time:
to foresee is to see before it happens. On a
noun it sets the thing in front: the forearm
is the front part of the arm, the foreword
is the words before the text.
forecast    fore + cast, thrown ahead
foresee     fore + see
forefather  fore + father
foreword    fore + word
The French twins are the words of the book
and the rank: foreword beside preface,
forefather beside ancestor, foremost beside
principal, forefront beside vanguard.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: fore- words.
The words for when and where are built like
the house words: two plain parts, the second
the thing, the first the kind. A waterfall
is a fall, of water. Nightfall is a fall too.
daytime     day + time
nightfall   night + fall
crossroads  cross + roads
seashore    sea + shore
The where-words are a set: some + where,
every + where, no + where. So are the sides:
lakeside, riverside, roadside. The French
twins belong to the map and the state:
seashore beside coast, hilltop beside summit,
homeland beside nation.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: when and where.
OUT- is Old English ut, out, and does two jobs.
On a verb it means beyond: to outdo is to do
more than the other. On a noun it means
outside or away: an outcast is cast out, an
outlaw stands outside the law.
outdo       out + do
outlast     out + last
outcast     out + cast
outlaw      out + law
The verb is the living one: outrun, outwit,
outbid, outnumber, outfox. Set out- on a verb
and it says more than the other. The French
twins: outlast beside endure, outcast beside
exile, outlive beside survive.
THE NEXT 25 CARDS: out- words.
A man named by his work: the herdsman tends
the herd, the helmsman holds the helm, the
spokesman speaks for the rest. Man was the
plain word for a person; the trade came first.
kinsman     kin + man
herdsman    herd + man
midwife     mid, with + wife, a woman
stepchild   step, bereaved + child
Two false friends. Midwife is not a middle
wife but the woman who is with you; step- is
Old English steop-, bereaved, so a stepchild
had lost a parent. The French twins are the
ranks: horseman beside cavalier, clergyman
beside minister, woodsman beside forester.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: kin, trades, the family.
OVER- is Old English ofer, above, across. It
sets the action above a thing or past it: to
overflow is to flow over the edge, to
overthrow is to throw down from power. Past a
limit it means too much: overwork, overreach.
overflow    over + flow
overthrow   over + throw
overtime    over + time, beyond the hours
overview    over + view, seen from above
One word turns on you: to overlook is to
look over a thing and so to miss it. The
French twins are the words of the court:
overthrow beside depose, overturn beside
reverse, overpower beside subdue.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: over- words.
UNDER is Old English under, beneath. It has
kept its plain sense: undergrowth is what
grows beneath the trees. Set on a verb it
means too little: underfed, underestimate.
understand  under + stand
undergrowth under + growth
underline   under + line
underdog    under + dog, the one beneath
The oldest three have drifted. To understand
is to stand beneath a thing and so to know
it; to undertake is to take a task upon
yourself; to undergo is to go under and
endure. Their French twins: undertake beside
attempt, undergo beside experience.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: under- words.
MIS- is Old English mis-, wrongly, badly. Set
on a verb it says the act went wrong: to
mistake is to take wrongly, to misread is to
read wrongly. On a noun it says bad: a mishap
is bad hap, bad luck, and misrule is bad rule.
mistake     mis + take
misread     mis + read
mishap      mis + hap, luck
misrule     mis + rule
The prefix is so alive that it sits on French
stems without a seam: misjudge, misfortune,
misquote. Where a French twin stands beside
the word it is the graver one: mistake beside
error, mishap beside accident.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: mis- words.
